sounds.name: SEM Brass
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s Oberheim synth brass
sounds.blurb: A bright, round brass voice with a soft swell at the front of every note.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths, one a few cents off, go through the 12 dB low-pass filter. ENV 2 opens the filter a little more slowly than the loudness rises, which gives the brassy swell. The SEM filter stays smooth even when it opens wide, which is why its brass sounds rounder than a Moog’s.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, slightly apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooth waves from XM1’s two oscillators go into its filter, one tuned a hair sharp. The slow beating between them is what makes one synth note sound more like a section than a single buzzy tone.
- VCO 1 and VCO 2 into VCF −4 (saw 80 %): the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) make the raw tone. The SEM has no level knobs: each VCO knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre, sends the sawtooth to the left and the pulse to the right. A saw carries every harmonic, the brassiest raw material.
- VCO 2 fine tune +0.6 (+12 cents): about an eighth of a semitone sharp. Too little to sound out of tune, enough to make the two waves drift against each other. More is wider and wobblier; at 0 the note goes narrow and static.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy note with a slow wobble in it. Set VCO 2 fine tune back to 0 and the wobble stops.

steps.title: Close the filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) trims the top off the two saws. Pulled well down, it leaves a dull, muted note, which is the resting point the envelope will open from in the next step.
- VCF frequency 4 (304 Hz): the cutoff. With NOTCH fully left, where it starts, the filter is low-pass: it keeps the lows and cuts the highs, so lower is darker. At about 300 Hz most of the buzz is gone.
- VCF resonance 2 (20 %): a small boost right at the cutoff. The SEM’s 12 dB (2-pole) filter stays smooth, so this adds a little roundness rather than a whistle.
- Listen for: the brightness from step 1 gone, leaving a soft, woolly note. Sweep FREQUENCY up and back to hear how much of the brass lives above the cutoff.

steps.title: Let ENV 2 open it
steps.why:
ENV 2 is XM1’s second envelope, a shape that rises and falls on every note. Its switch under the VCF MODULATION knob starts at ENV 2, so turning the knob lets it open the cutoff as each note starts and settle back: the swell that makes a note sound blown rather than switched on.
- VCF modulation +2.8 (+2.9 oct): how far ENV 2 lifts the cutoff above 304 Hz at its peak, almost three octaves. More gives a brighter, brassier bite; left of centre would close the filter instead.
- ENV 2 attack 3.5 (43 ms): how long the filter takes to open. It is slower than the loudness, so each note swells into brightness. Shorter gives a harder “blat”.
- ENV 2 decay 5 (500 ms), sustain 4 (40 %): after the peak the filter falls over half a second to 40 % of the way up and holds there. DECAY also sets the release (390 ms).
- Listen for: a “waah” at the start of each note, then a mellower tone while you hold it. Turn ENV 2 attack to 0 and the swell becomes a sharp bark.

steps.title: Shape the loudness
steps.why:
ENV 1 shapes the loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). The SEM envelopes have only ATTACK, DECAY and SUSTAIN: with sustain at full, DECAY only matters as the fade after you let go.
- ENV 1 attack 2 (14 ms): a softened start that takes the click off, still quicker than the 43 ms filter swell so the brightness arrives just after the note.
- ENV 1 decay 4.5 (350 ms, release 270 ms): held notes do not fade; when you lift the key the note tails off over about a quarter of a second rather than stopping dead. Longer suits slow chords; shorter is tighter for stabs.
- ENV 1 sustain 10 (100 %): full level for as long as the key is down, so long brass chords keep their weight.
- Listen for: the end of each note. Short stabs finish with a gentle fall-off instead of a click; set ATTACK back to 0 and the front of each note gets a harder edge.

sounds.name: Notch Sweep
sounds.ref: The SEM’s own filter trick
sounds.blurb: A held chord whose tone is carved by a notch that sweeps slowly up and down.
sounds.how: The NOTCH knob at the centre turns the filter into a notch: it takes a slice out of the sound and keeps everything above and below. Each module’s LFO sweeps its own cutoff, so the notch moves through the harmonics like a slow phaser. DUO puts the two notes on separate modules, each with its own notch.

steps.title: One note on each module
steps.why:
The 2-XM is two complete synths, XM1 and XM2, side by side. This step switches the second one on and shares your notes between them, so a two-note chord becomes two separate voices.
- ASSIGN DUO: decides how notes reach the two modules. DUO gives each new key to whichever module is free, so hold two keys and XM1 takes one, XM2 the other. UNI would put every note on both; SPLIT divides the keyboard at middle C.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0, silent whatever its own panel does. At 7 it matches XM1.
- Listen for: hold two keys. Both notes now sound, each a plain bright sawtooth from the modules’ starting settings. Pull XM2 level back to 0 and one of them disappears.

steps.title: Bright sawtooths into both filters
steps.why:
Each module now gets two slightly detuned sawtooths. A notch filter can only take out harmonics that are there, and saws are full of them.
- VCO 1 −4 (saw 80 %), VCO 2 −3 (saw 60 %): the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) make the tone. The knobs for them in the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) section are silent at the centre, saw to the left, pulse to the right. VCO 1 leads and VCO 2 sits a little under it, on both modules.
- VCO 2 fine tune +0.5 (+10 cents): a tenth of a semitone sharp on each module, so each note beats gently and sounds wider.
- Listen for: a fuller, buzzier chord with a slow wobble on each note. Turn one module’s VCO 2 knob back to the centre to hear how much thickness it adds.

steps.title: NOTCH to the centre
steps.why:
The SEM filter’s NOTCH knob sweeps smoothly from low-pass through notch to high-pass. At the centre it cuts a slice out of the sound and keeps everything above and below, which sounds hollow and phasey rather than darker.
- NOTCH 0 (notch), both modules: fully left is low-pass, where it started; fully right is high-pass. Left of centre the sound goes darker, right of centre thinner.
- VCF frequency 5.5 (843 Hz): where the notch sits. Around 840 Hz it scoops out the middle, leaving the low body and the top fizz.
- VCF resonance 3.5 (35 %): makes the notch more pronounced and sharper. At 0 it is subtle.
- Listen for: a hollow, scooped chord. Turn FREQUENCY slowly by hand and hear the notch move through the harmonics like a phaser. The next step does that for you.

steps.title: Sweep it with the LFO
steps.why:
An LFO (low-frequency oscillator) is a slow wave used to move a setting rather than to be heard. Here each module’s LFO sweeps its own cutoff, so the notch travels up and down by itself.
- VCF modulation source LFO: the switch under the filter’s MODULATION knob picks what moves the cutoff. It starts at ENV 2, the filter envelope.
- VCF modulation +2.8 (+2.9 oct): how far the LFO swings the cutoff, and the notch with it, nearly three octaves. Less gives a subtler sweep.
- XM1 LFO 0.40 Hz, XM2 0.52 Hz: one sweep every two to two and a half seconds. The slightly different speeds let the two notches drift apart and back together.
- Listen for: hold a chord and hear the hollow band move up and down, each note at its own pace. Turn one LFO faster and the slow phaser turns into a wobble.

steps.title: Long notes
steps.why:
ENV 1 is the envelope that shapes loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). Set to hold, it keeps the chord sounding long enough to hear the notch make its full journey.
- ENV 1 attack 3 (29 ms): a soft start, without the click of an instant attack.
- ENV 1 decay 6 (1.0 s, release 800 ms): on the SEM, DECAY also sets the release. With full sustain it only acts after you let go, so chords fade over most of a second.
- ENV 1 sustain 10 (100 %): held notes stay at full level, on both modules.
- Listen for: the tail after you release the chord, with the notch still moving as it fades. Turn DECAY down and the chord stops short.

sounds.name: Two-Voice Counterpoint
sounds.ref: In the style of Kyle Dixon and Michael Stein — "Stranger Things" theme
sounds.blurb: A plucked arpeggio and a held bass note, each on its own module and its own side of the stereo.
sounds.how: DUO gives each new key to the module that is free, so a held bass note stays on one module while the arpeggio moves on the other. Both modules have the same short, plucky filter envelope. Panning them apart makes the two parts easy to hear.

steps.title: DUO, both modules up
steps.why:
The 2-XM is two synths in one, XM1 and XM2. DUO shares the keys between them, so a held bass note and a moving line play on separate modules, and panning puts each on its own side.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free. Hold a bass note and it stays on its module while the next notes go to the other.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0 and is silent until it is brought up.
- XM1 pan −3, XM2 pan +3: 60 % towards the left and right. Two parts that sit apart are much easier to follow.
- Listen for: hold one low key and play a few notes above it. The held note stays on one side and the moving notes come from the other.

steps.title: A pulse and a sawtooth
steps.why:
Each module gets a narrow pulse on top and a sawtooth an octave below, set the same on both. The low saw gives body; the pulse gives a woody, reedy edge for the arpeggio.
- VCO 1 into VCF +3.5 (pulse 70 %): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes the tone. Its knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre; right of centre sends the pulse wave.
- VCO 1 pulse width 35 %: narrower than a square (50 %), so it sounds thinner and more nasal than a hollow, clarinet-like square.
- VCO 2 −2.5 (saw 50 %), FREQ 3 (−12 st): a quieter saw, an octave down. On FREQUENCY two numbers is an octave, and 5 is the starting pitch.
- Listen for: a fuller, lower note with a reedy buzz on top. Turn VCO 2’s knob to the centre and the note loses its bottom octave.

steps.title: Pluck the filters
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sets the brightness, and ENV 2, the second envelope, flicks it open on every note. With no sustain, each note starts bright and closes straight away: a pluck.
- FREQ 3.2 (176 Hz), RES 4: a dark low-pass resting point, with enough resonance to give the pluck a round, rubbery edge.
- VCF modulation +3 (+3.3 oct): how far ENV 2 opens the cutoff at the start of each note. More is a brighter, snappier pluck; less is duller.
- ENV 2 A 3 ms, D 280 ms, S 0: opens at once, closes again in about a quarter of a second, holds nothing. DECAY sets the pluck length; longer turns it into a “wow”.
- Listen for: a bright “tick” on each note that falls to a dull thud. Play the arpeggio and sweep ENV 2 decay on both modules to lengthen and shorten the pluck.

steps.title: Let the notes ring a little
steps.why:
ENV 1 sets the loudness of each note through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). The filter has closed by now, but the volume carries on, so the held bass keeps sounding as a dark tone under the arpeggio.
- ENV 1 decay 5 (500 ms, release 390 ms): after the attack the level falls over half a second to the sustain level. On the SEM, DECAY also sets how long a note takes to die away after you let go.
- ENV 1 sustain 7 (70 %): held notes stay at 70 %, so the bass keeps its place under the moving line. At 0 it would die away by itself.
- Listen for: the held bass carrying on, a little quieter after its attack, and arpeggio notes trailing off over a few hundred milliseconds when released rather than cutting dead.

sounds.name: Split Bass and Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of a 1970s funk keyboard split
sounds.blurb: A punchy bass under the left hand and a singing, gliding lead under the right.
sounds.how: SPLIT sends keys below middle C to XM1 and the rest to XM2, so the two modules become two instruments. XM1 is a short, dark bass; XM2 is a brighter lead with portamento. The Two Voice was often played this way, one hand on each module.

steps.title: Split the keyboard
steps.why:
SPLIT turns the 2-XM’s two modules into two instruments on one keyboard: XM1 under the left hand, XM2 under the right.
- ASSIGN SPLIT: keys below middle C play XM1, the rest play XM2. UNI puts both modules on every note and DUO shares them out as you play.
- XM2 level 6.5 (65 %): XM2 starts at 0; at 6.5 it sits just under XM1, which stays at 7.
- Listen for: play low, then high. Both halves sound the same for now, the plain starting sawtooth, until the next two steps give each its own sound.

steps.title: XM1: a round bass
steps.why:
XM1 becomes the bass: a sawtooth with a pulse an octave under it, through a dark filter that snaps open on each note, and a volume that dips once the note has hit.
- VCO 1 saw 80 %, VCO 2 pulse 60 %: the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) are mixed by their knobs in the VCF section, saw to the left, pulse to the right. The saw gives bite, the pulse body.
- VCO 2 frequency 3 (−12 st): an octave down, for weight in the low end.
- FREQ 3 (154 Hz), RES 3: the VCF (filter) sits low in low-pass, so the bass is dark and round.
- VCF MOD +3.3 oct, ENV 2 D 210 ms, S 0: ENV 2, the filter envelope, flicks the cutoff up and back down in about a fifth of a second. That is the punch.
- ENV 1 D 170 ms, S 60 %: ENV 1, the loudness envelope, drops to 60 % after the hit and releases in 130 ms, so notes stay tight.
- Listen for: a short “dow” on each low note. Lengthen ENV 2 decay to hear it turn into a slower “wow”.

steps.title: XM2: a gliding lead
steps.why:
XM2 becomes the lead: two sawtooths a fifth apart, a fairly open filter, and a glide between notes.
- VCO 1 saw 80 %, VCO 2 saw 50 %: both as saws, VCO 2 quieter so it colours rather than doubles.
- VCO 2 frequency 6.2 (+7 st): a fifth up, so every note sounds as an open interval, a classic fusion lead colour.
- FREQ 6.5 (1.7 kHz), MOD +1.5 (+1.2 oct): fairly bright, with ENV 2 adding a little extra brightness at the start of each note.
- ENV 2 decay 5 (500 ms): the brightness settles over half a second to ENV 2’s sustain level, still at its starting 40 %.
- ON, XM2 PORTAMENTO 3.5 (370 ms): the switch turns glide on for both modules and each module’s knob sets its own time. XM1’s stays at 0, so the bass does not slide.
- Listen for: play two notes above middle C in turn and hear the pitch slide between them over about a third of a second.

steps.title: Vibrato on the lead
steps.why:
XM2’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves a setting) adds vibrato to the lead only. XM1 has its own LFO, which is not used, so the bass stays steady.
- XM2 VCO 1 modulation −0.9 (FM +0.8 st): left of centre is FREQ, pitch modulation (FM on the chip means frequency modulation). A touch left gives a gentle vibrato; further left gets seasick. Right of centre would move pulse width instead.
- XM2 VCO 1 modulation source LFO: the switch under the knob. It starts at ENV 1.
- XM2 LFO rate 5.8 (3.89 Hz): about four wobbles a second, a natural singing speed.
- Listen for: hold a lead note and hear the pitch waver while the bass below stays still. Only VCO 1 moves; VCO 2’s fifth holds steady underneath.

sounds.name: Four-Oscillator Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s jazz-fusion synth leads
sounds.blurb: A huge, gliding mono lead: four oscillators on every note, spread across the stereo.
sounds.how: UNI plays each note on both modules, so four oscillators sound at once. Detuning them slightly against each other, and panning the modules apart, gives a wide, moving tone. Portamento on both makes the line slide.

steps.title: Both modules on every note
steps.why:
UNI plays every note on both modules at once, so each note gets four oscillators: two from XM1 and two from XM2. Panning the modules apart makes the lead wide.
- ASSIGN UNI: both modules play each note. It is where the switch starts; a second held key would go to XM2 alone.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): up from 0, so XM2 is now heard, matching XM1.
- XM1 pan −2.5, XM2 pan +2.5: each module 50 % to its side.
- Listen for: the note getting louder and a little wider. Both modules are still on their starting settings, so for now the width comes mostly from the pan.

steps.title: Four sawtooths, all slightly apart
steps.why:
All four VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) go in as sawtooths, each tuned slightly differently. Four saws beating against each other give the thick, moving tone of a big unison lead.
- VCO 1 and VCO 2 −4 (saw 80 %): the knobs in the VCF (filter) section, silent at the centre, saw to the left.
- XM1 VCO 2 fine +0.5 (+10 cents): XM1’s pair beats slowly.
- XM2 fine −8 and +18 cents: XM2’s pair sits either side of XM1, one flat and one sharper. The spread across four pitches is the width; with the pan it also moves between the speakers.
- Listen for: a thick, chorused note that swirls from side to side. Pull XM2 level to 0 and the lead goes half as thick.

steps.title: A bright filter with a push
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) takes some fizz off the four saws but stays fairly open, and ENV 2, the filter envelope, adds a push of extra brightness at the start of each note.
- VCF frequency 6.4 (1.6 kHz): low-pass, bright enough to cut through a mix, with the harshest top trimmed.
- VCF resonance 2.5 (25 %): a small lift at the cutoff that makes the tone slightly vocal.
- VCF MOD +1.8 (+1.5 oct), ENV 2 D 500 ms: each note opens an octave and a half higher and settles over half a second to ENV 2’s sustain, still at its starting 40 %.
- Listen for: a brighter front on each note, then a steadier tone. Set VCF modulation to 0 on both modules and the attacks lose their push.

steps.title: Glide
steps.why:
Portamento makes the pitch slide from one note to the next instead of jumping. The same time on both modules keeps all four oscillators sliding together.
- Portamento ON: the master switch for both modules’ glide.
- XM1 and XM2 portamento 3 (270 ms): about a quarter of a second per slide. Longer is more dramatic; shorter is barely a scoop.
- Listen for: play a leap and hear the lead slide up to it. Set XM2’s portamento a little longer than XM1’s and the two halves arrive at different moments, which smears the note.

sounds.name: Sync Tear
sounds.ref: In the style of late-1970s synth-rock sync leads
sounds.blurb: A lead whose tone tears downwards at the start of every note.
sounds.how: SYNC locks VCO 2 to VCO 1, so VCO 2’s pitch changes its tone, not its note. VCO 2’s MODULATION, turned left with ENV 2 as its source, pushes VCO 2 up at the start of each note and lets it fall back, which sweeps the tone: the classic sync tear.

steps.title: Only VCO 2, synced
steps.why:
Only XM1 plays here, and only VCO 2, locked to VCO 1 with hard sync. That lets VCO 2’s tuning knob change the tone of the note instead of its pitch.
- VCO 1 into VCF 0 (off): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. VCO 1’s knob in the VCF (filter) section goes to the centre, which is silent. VCO 1 still runs and drives the sync; it just is not heard.
- VCO 2 into VCF −4.5 (saw 90 %): VCO 2 in as a sawtooth.
- VCO 2 sync On: VCO 2 restarts every time VCO 1 does, so the note follows VCO 1’s pitch.
- VCO 2 frequency 6.5 (+9 st): tuned above VCO 1, which adds a harsh, nasal peak to the tone rather than raising the note.
- Listen for: turn VCO 2 FREQUENCY slowly while holding a note. The pitch stays put while the tone snarls and tears.

steps.title: Sweep VCO 2 with ENV 2
steps.why:
ENV 2, XM1’s second envelope, now bends VCO 2’s pitch on every note. Under sync that sweep is heard as the tone tearing down from a scream to the steadier tone set in step 1.
- VCO 2 modulation −3.2 (FM +9.8 st): left of centre moves pitch (FREQ; FM means frequency modulation). At the start of each note VCO 2 is pushed nearly ten semitones higher. Further left is a longer, more dramatic tear; right of centre would move pulse width instead.
- VCO 2 modulation source ENV 2: the switch under the knob. It can also be E+V (the envelope scaled by how hard you play) or the LFO.
- ENV 2 A 0, D 720 ms, S 15 %: an instant jump, then a fall over most of a second to just above the resting tone. DECAY sets how long the tear takes.
- Listen for: a “neeow” on each note. Short decays give a bark; long ones a slow, sweeping snarl.

steps.title: Open filter
steps.why:
The sweep is the sound, so the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) stays fairly open and only takes the harshest top off. Its MODULATION is still at the centre, so nothing moves the cutoff.
- VCF frequency 7 (2.3 kHz): the cutoff, in low-pass. It starts at 8 (4.6 kHz); bringing it down a notch softens the fizz. Much lower and the tear gets muffled.
- VCF resonance 1.5 (15 %): a slight lift at the cutoff for a touch of edge.
- Listen for: the tear still clear but less brittle. Pull FREQUENCY down to 4 to hear how much of the effect lives in the upper harmonics.

sounds.name: Mega-City Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of Geoff Barrow and Ben Salisbury — Drokk
sounds.blurb: A dark, slowly shifting drone that plays by itself, with a pulse moving underneath.
sounds.how: Both VCAs are set to ON/EXT, so the modules sound with no key held. Each has two sawtooths an octave apart and slightly out of tune, through a low-pass filter that its own slow LFO opens and closes. The two LFOs run at different speeds, so the drone never repeats exactly. Playing a key just changes the note.

steps.title: Hold both amplifiers open
steps.why:
Both modules are made to sound all the time, with no key held. That is the basis of a drone that plays itself.
- XM1 and XM2 VCA mode ON/EXT: the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) is the volume stage. At ENV it only opens while ENV 1 runs on a note; at ON/EXT it stays open, unless a cable in VCA CV takes over (there is none here).
- XM2 level 6 (60 %): XM2 starts at 0; at 6 it sits a little under XM1.
- Listen for: sound starting straight away without touching a key. Set one VCA switch back to ENV and that module goes quiet until you play.

steps.title: Low, beating sawtooths
steps.why:
Each module gets two sawtooths, the second an octave down and a little sharp, so the drone beats slowly. XM2 is pitched a fifth above XM1, giving an open, bleak interval.
- VCO 1 and VCO 2 −4 (saw 80 %): the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) go into the VCF (filter) as saws.
- VCO 2 −12 st (XM1), −5 st (XM2): XM1’s VCO 2 is an octave below its VCO 1. XM2’s sits five semitones down, an octave under XM2’s raised VCO 1.
- VCO 2 fine +0.4 (+8 cents): a slight detune on each pair, for slow beating.
- XM2 VCO 1 frequency 6.2 (+7 st): a fifth above XM1.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzy fifth with a slow wobble. Set XM2 level to 0 to hear XM1’s octave on its own.

steps.title: Dark filters
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) goes well down on both modules, so only the bottom of the drone gets through: dark, heavy and close.
- VCF frequency 3.4 (202 Hz): low-pass at about 200 Hz, cutting away most of the buzz.
- VCF resonance 5 (50 %): a clear lift at the cutoff that gives the dark tone a hollow hum and makes the coming sweeps easier to hear. The SEM filter stays round even here.
- Listen for: the drone turning from a bright buzz into a low rumble with a ring near the cutoff. Sweep FREQUENCY by hand to preview what the LFOs will do next.

steps.title: Slow, separate sweeps
steps.why:
Each module’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves a setting) opens and closes its own filter. The two run at different speeds, so the sweeps drift in and out of step and the drone never repeats exactly.
- VCF MOD source LFO, MOD +3.5 (+4.1 oct): the switch sends the LFO to the cutoff and the knob sets how far it swings, about four octaves. Less gives a gentler movement.
- XM1 LFO 0.24 Hz, XM2 0.33 Hz: one sweep about every four seconds on XM1 and every three on XM2.
- XM1 pan −3, XM2 pan +3: the modules 60 % to opposite sides, so the two sweeps move across the stereo.
- Listen for: a slow rise and fall on each side that goes in and out of step. Play a key to change the note; the sweeps carry on.

sounds.name: Bubbling Blips
sounds.ref: In the style of Mark Mothersbaugh — The Life Aquatic score
sounds.blurb: Light, watery blips that bubble up and down in pitch.
sounds.how: The band-pass filter with plenty of resonance turns each note into a round, liquid tone. VCO 1’s MODULATION, turned left with the LFO as its source, wobbles the pitch fast and wide, and ENV 2 pings the filter on every note. DUO lets two blips overlap on the two modules.

steps.title: Band-pass, ringing
steps.why:
The filter is switched to band-pass and made to ring. That takes the plain starting sawtooth and keeps only a narrow, resonant band: a round, watery tone.
- XM1 VCF response BP: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) normally sweeps from low-pass to high-pass with NOTCH. BP (band-pass) lets only a band around the cutoff through, and NOTCH then does nothing.
- VCF resonance 7.5 (75 %): high, so the band rings. Less is duller; the SEM filter stays smooth even up here.
- VCF frequency 6 (1.2 kHz): the centre of the band.
- Listen for: a thin, hollow, whistling tone in place of the full saw. Sweep FREQUENCY to hear the band move like a wah.

steps.title: A pluck on the filter
steps.why:
ENV 2, the filter envelope, pings the band upwards at the start of each note, and ENV 1, the loudness envelope, now lets every note die away by itself. Together they turn a steady tone into a short blip.
- VCF modulation +2.5 (+2.5 oct): how far ENV 2 lifts the band on each note.
- ENV 2 A 0, D 170 ms, S 0: an instant jump and a quick fall, with nothing held.
- ENV 1 decay 4.2 (280 ms), sustain 0: through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), the volume falls to silence in about a quarter of a second even with the key held.
- Listen for: a “bloop” on each note, the ring dropping in pitch as the band falls. A longer ENV 2 decay makes it more of a wah.

steps.title: Wobble the pitch
steps.why:
XM1’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves a setting), running fast, now wobbles VCO 1’s pitch. With the ringing band on top, that is the bubbling.
- VCO 1 modulation −2 (FM +3.8 st): left of centre moves pitch (FREQ; FM means frequency modulation), here by nearly four semitones. Nearer the centre it becomes a gentle vibrato.
- VCO 1 modulation source LFO: the switch starts at ENV 1.
- XM1 LFO rate 6.8 (7.30 Hz): about seven wobbles a second, fast enough to bubble rather than sway.
- VCO 1 into VCF +3.5 (pulse 70 %): VCO 1 (voltage-controlled oscillator) swaps from saw to pulse, right of centre on its knob, a hollower source for the band to ring on.
- Listen for: each blip warbling up and down. Turn the LFO rate down and the bubble slows into a siren.

steps.title: Two at once
steps.why:
XM2 gets the same blip, panned the other way, and DUO shares the notes between the two, so a quick line bounces between the sides and blips can overlap instead of cutting each other off.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free.
- XM2 level 7, pan +3; XM1 pan −3: XM2 brought in from 0 and the two placed 60 % to either side.
- XM2 VCF BP, resonance 7.5, 1.2 kHz: the same ringing band as XM1, with VCF modulation +2.5 for the ping.
- XM2 ENV 2 and ENV 1 as XM1: 170 ms filter ping, 280 ms loudness, no sustain.
- XM2 VCO 1 pulse, LFO 9.40 Hz: slightly faster than XM1’s 7.30 Hz, so the two bubble differently.
- Listen for: play a quick run and hear blips land left and right, each ringing on as the next starts.

sounds.name: Two-Voice Strings
sounds.ref: In the style of late-1970s Oberheim string sounds
sounds.blurb: Soft, shimmering two-note strings that swell in and fade out.
sounds.how: Each module plays two pulse waves whose widths are swept by its own LFO through the MODULATION knobs, which gives the shimmer of a string section. DUO puts each note of an interval on its own module, and the slow ENV 1 attack makes each note swell in.

steps.title: DUO, both modules
steps.why:
DUO puts each note of a two-note interval on its own module, which the string shimmer needs: each note gets its own oscillators and LFO.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free. Hold two keys and XM1 takes one, XM2 the other. UNI would put both modules on every note.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0, silent whatever its panel does. At 7 it matches XM1.
- XM1 pan −2, XM2 pan +2: 40 % to each side, enough to separate the notes without splitting them wide.
- Listen for: hold two keys and hear both, slightly apart in the stereo. Both modules still give the plain starting sawtooth.

steps.title: Pulse waves
steps.why:
Both modules switch from saw to pulse waves. A pulse at its starting 50 % is a square: hollow and woody, fewer harmonics than a saw, and the raw material for the shimmer in the next step.
- VCO 1 pulse 70 %, VCO 2 pulse 60 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The knobs in the VCF (filter) section are silent at the centre and send the pulse to the right.
- VCO 2 fine tune +0.6 (+12 cents): about an eighth of a semitone sharp on each module, so the two pulses beat slowly.
- Listen for: a hollower, softer tone than the saw, with a gentle wobble from the detune. Turn VCO 2 fine to 0 on one module and that note goes still.

steps.title: Sweep the widths
steps.why:
PWM (pulse-width modulation) is the string shimmer: each module’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves a setting) keeps changing the width of all four pulses, so the tone never sits still.
- VCO 1 PWM 40 %, VCO 2 PWM 32 %: right of centre moves pulse width rather than pitch. More gives a deeper, more obvious sweep; VCO 2 moves a little less so the pair does not move in lockstep.
- VCO 1 and VCO 2 modulation source LFO: the switches start on the envelopes; at LFO the width moves continuously.
- XM1 LFO 0.85 Hz, XM2 1.10 Hz: about one sweep a second, slightly different on each module, so the two notes shimmer independently.
- Listen for: a slow, choral movement in each note. Set one VCO 1 modulation to the centre and hear that part of the movement stop.

steps.title: Soft and slow
steps.why:
The filter takes the edge off the pulses, and ENV 1, the loudness envelope, makes each note swell in and fade out slowly, as a bowed string section would.
- VCF frequency 6 (1.2 kHz), both modules: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in low-pass comes down from its starting 4.6 kHz, so the strings are softer and sit behind other parts.
- ENV 1 attack 6.8 (530 ms): each note takes about half a second to reach full level. Shorter is more like a string stab.
- ENV 1 D 1.5 s, S 100 %: held notes stay at full, and on the SEM DECAY also sets the release, so notes fade over more than a second when you let go.
- Listen for: each chord swelling up and dying away gently after you release it. Play fast notes and hear them blur into each other.

sounds.name: Cross-Patched Wobble
sounds.ref: A patchbay lesson: one module modulating the other
sounds.blurb: A growling bass whose filter is wobbled by the other module’s LFO.
sounds.how: XM2 is not heard at all (its LEVEL stays at 0), but its LFO is patched into XM1’s VCF CV input. With XM1’s filter modulation switch at EXT, that LFO moves XM1’s cutoff, while XM1’s own LFO stays free for vibrato. It is the simplest way to use one module as a modulation source for the other.

steps.title: A heavy bass on XM1
steps.why:
XM1 is set up as a heavy bass. XM2 stays silent in this sound; only its LFO gets used, later, through a cable.
- VCO 1 saw 80 %, VCO 2 pulse 70 %: the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) mixed by their knobs in the VCF section, saw to the left, pulse to the right.
- VCO 2 frequency 3 (−12 st): the pulse an octave down, for weight in the low end.
- FREQ 3.6 (232 Hz), RES 6: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in low-pass, set dark, with a strong ring at the cutoff that will make the wobble growl.
- ENV 1 decay 5 (500 ms), sustain 8 (80 %): ENV 1 shapes the loudness. Held notes settle to 80 %, and DECAY also gives a 390 ms release.
- Listen for: a dark, round bass with a hum at the cutoff. Sweep FREQUENCY by hand; the wobble will do this automatically.

steps.title: Patch XM2’s LFO into XM1’s filter
steps.why:
The patchbay lets one module control the other. This cable carries XM2’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow triangle wave, to the input that can move XM1’s cutoff.
- Cable XM2 LFO → XM1 VCF CV: CV means control voltage. VCF CV only affects XM1’s filter when XM1’s VCF modulation switch is at EXT, which it is not yet.
- XM2 LFO rate: still at its starting 2.35 Hz. XM2’s level is 0, so none of XM2’s sound is heard; the LFO runs anyway.
- Listen for: no change at all. That is the point: a patched cable does nothing until the destination is listening.

steps.title: Listen to EXT
steps.why:
XM1’s filter now follows the cable. The EXT position of the modulation switch takes its signal from VCF CV, so XM2’s LFO sweeps XM1’s cutoff up and down.
- XM1 VCF modulation source EXT: with no cable in VCF CV, EXT would give ENV 2 scaled by velocity. With the cable in, it uses the cable. XM1’s own LFO stays free for other jobs.
- XM1 VCF modulation +3.4 (+3.9 oct): how deep the wobble is, almost four octaves of swing. Less is a gentle movement; left of centre flips it upside down.
- Listen for: a “wub-wub” on every held note at about two cycles a second. Turn MODULATION towards the centre and the wobble shrinks.

steps.title: Set the wobble speed on XM2
steps.why:
The speed of the wobble is set on XM2’s panel, even though XM2 is silent. Using one module purely as a modulation source for the other is the basic cross-patch lesson.
- XM2 LFO rate 5.2 (2.66 Hz): a little faster than the starting 2.35 Hz. Higher gives a faster, busier wobble; lower gives a slow, heavy one.
- Listen for: turn XM2’s LFO rate while holding a note and hear XM1’s wobble speed up and slow down. Pull the cable and the wobble stops; EXT falls back to ENV 2 scaled by velocity.

sounds.name: Velocity Funk Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s funk synth bass
sounds.blurb: A snappy bass that gets brighter and louder the harder each note is played.
sounds.how: The E+V positions scale the envelopes by velocity. With the VCA at E+V, harder notes are louder; with the VCF switch at EXT and nothing patched, harder notes open the filter further. The riff has accents on the beat, so you can hear the difference.

steps.title: Saw and pulse
steps.why:
XM1’s two oscillators become a funk bass source: a bright sawtooth for bite with a narrow pulse an octave under it for weight.
- VCO 1 into VCF −4 (saw 80 %): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The SEM has no level knobs; each VCO knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre, saw to the left, pulse to the right.
- VCO 2 +3 (pulse 60 %), FREQ 3 (−12 st): the pulse, an octave down. On FREQUENCY two numbers is an octave, and 5 is the starting pitch.
- VCO 2 pulse width 30 %: narrower than a square, so the low octave has a reedy, nasal edge rather than a hollow one, which helps it cut through on small speakers.
- Listen for: a loud, buzzy low note with plenty of top. Turn VCO 2’s knob to the centre and the bottom octave drops out.

steps.title: A snappy filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) goes dark, and ENV 2, the filter envelope, snaps it open at the start of every note and shuts it again. That is the funk “pow”.
- VCF frequency 3 (154 Hz): low-pass, low enough that the resting tone is a dull thump.
- VCF resonance 4 (40 %): a lift at the cutoff that makes the snap sound rubbery and vocal. The SEM’s 2-pole filter keeps it round.
- VCF modulation +3.2 (+3.6 oct): how far ENV 2 lifts the cutoff on each note. More is brighter and snappier.
- ENV 2 A 0, D 250 ms, S 0: opens at once, closes in a quarter of a second, holds nothing. DECAY is the length of the snap.
- Listen for: every note with the same bright “pow” then a dark body, however hard you play. The next step changes that.

steps.title: Velocity on the filter
steps.why:
One switch makes the filter follow your playing. On the SEM, the EXT position of the VCF modulation switch, with no cable in VCF CV, gives ENV 2 scaled by velocity: how hard you hit the key.
- VCF modulation source EXT: soft notes now open the filter only a little and stay dark; hard notes open it the full +3.6 octaves set by the MODULATION knob. With a cable in VCF CV, EXT would follow that instead.
- Listen for: play the riff with accents on the beat. Accented notes bark, the notes between them stay muted and round. That contrast is the groove. Switch back to ENV 2 and every note is the same again.

steps.title: Velocity on the loudness
steps.why:
The VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) sets the loudness, and E+V makes it follow velocity too, so accents now jump out in level as well as brightness. ENV 1 is shortened to keep the bass tight.
- VCA mode E+V: ENV 1 shapes each note, scaled by how hard you play. At ENV every note is equally loud; ON/EXT would hold it open.
- ENV 1 decay 4.2 (280 ms, release 220 ms): after the hit the level falls over about a quarter of a second, and DECAY also sets the fade after you let go.
- ENV 1 sustain 6 (60 %): held notes settle to 60 %, so the attack stands out above the body.
- Listen for: ghost notes sitting quietly under the accents. Play one note softly then hard to hear both the level and the brightness jump.

sounds.name: Falling Synth Tom
sounds.ref: In the style of late-1970s disco synth drums
sounds.blurb: A round electronic tom whose pitch drops as it dies away.
sounds.how: VCO 1’s MODULATION, turned left with ENV 1 as its source, pushes the pitch up at the start of each hit and lets it fall with the envelope. ENV 1 has no sustain, so each hit dies away by itself. A little noise adds the stick.

steps.title: One plain wave
steps.why:
A drum starts from a simple, pure tone. XM1 plays one square wave through a filter pulled down enough to take off the fizz.
- VCO 1 into VCF +4 (pulse 80 %): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Its knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre; right of centre sends the pulse. The pulse width is still at 50 %, which makes it a square: hollow, round, few harmonics. VCO 2 stays at the centre, out of the sound.
- VCF frequency 5 (600 Hz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in low-pass. Down from its starting 4.6 kHz, so the square is soft and woody, closer to a drum skin than a buzz.
- Listen for: a steady, dull organ-like tone. It becomes a drum in the next two steps.

steps.title: A falling pitch
steps.why:
VCO 1’s MODULATION knob, with ENV 1 as its source, will push the pitch up at the start of each hit and let it fall with the envelope. ENV 1 is the envelope that also shapes the loudness.
- VCO 1 modulation −2.8 (FM +7.5 st): left of centre moves pitch (FREQ; FM means frequency modulation). At the envelope’s peak the note is seven and a half semitones higher. More gives a bigger drop; right of centre would move pulse width instead.
- VCO 1 modulation source ENV 1: where the switch starts; the other choices are E+V and LFO.
- Listen for: each note now sounds higher, with a tiny upward chirp at the start. ENV 1 is still at full sustain, so the pitch stays up; the drop arrives in the next step when sustain goes to 0.

steps.title: Make it a hit
steps.why:
ENV 1 is turned into a hit: instant start, no hold, and a short fade. Because the same envelope bends the pitch, the pitch falls as the tom dies away.
- ENV 1 attack 0 (3 ms): full level at once, so the tom has a sharp front.
- ENV 1 decay 4.8 (440 ms, release 330 ms): the length of the hit and of the pitch drop together. Shorter is a tight, dry tom; longer a deep, booming one.
- ENV 1 sustain 0: every note dies away by itself, even with the key held, as a drum does.
- Listen for: a “pyoom” that drops in pitch as it fades. Play a descending fill and sweep ENV 1 decay to hear the toms go from dry to boomy.

steps.title: A touch of noise
steps.why:
A little white noise adds the stick hitting the skin. It goes through the same VCA and ENV 1, so it only sounds with each hit.
- EXT/noise knob +1.2 (noise 24 %): the third knob in the VCF section is silent at the centre, brings in the external input to the left and white noise to the right. A little keeps the tone in front; more turns the tom into a thud with hiss.
- Listen for: a soft “tsh” at the front of each hit, fading with it. Turn the knob to the centre and the tom loses its attack and sounds softer and rounder.

sounds.name: Wind
sounds.ref: A classic synth sound effect
sounds.blurb: Gusting wind, made from noise and a slowly moving band-pass filter.
sounds.how: The EXT knob turned right brings in white noise, and both VCO knobs are at the centre, so noise is all there is. The band-pass filter with resonance picks out a whistling band, and the slow LFO moves it up and down like gusts.

steps.title: Noise only
steps.why:
Wind is made from noise, not pitch. XM1’s oscillator is taken out and the noise source brought in on its own.
- VCO 1 into VCF 0 (off): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes pitched tone. Its knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre, so no pitch gets through.
- EXT/noise knob +5 (noise 100 %): the third knob in the VCF section is silent at the centre, brings in the external input to the left and white noise to the right. Fully right is all noise, every frequency at once.
- Listen for: a steady hiss while a key is held. The key no longer changes anything but the timing.

steps.title: A whistling band
steps.why:
The band-pass filter picks a narrow band out of the noise and resonance makes it whistle, the way wind whistles through a gap.
- VCF response BP: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) switches to BP, band-pass, which lets only a band around the cutoff through. The NOTCH knob then does nothing.
- VCF resonance 8 (80 %): how much the band whistles. Low gives a broad rush; high gives a thin, pitched howl.
- VCF frequency 6 (1.2 kHz): where the band sits, in the middle of the range. Higher is a thin whistle, lower a dull roar.
- Listen for: the hiss narrowed into a breathy whistle. Sweep FREQUENCY by hand to hear the wind rise and fall.

steps.title: Gusts
steps.why:
XM1’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves a setting) now moves the band up and down, like gusts.
- VCF modulation source LFO: the switch under the filter’s MODULATION knob. It starts at ENV 2.
- VCF modulation +3.5 (+4.1 oct): how far the band swings, about four octaves. More gives bigger gusts; less a gentle breeze.
- XM1 LFO rate 2 (0.35 Hz): one rise and fall about every three seconds. Faster sounds like a storm; slower like a steady draught.
- Listen for: the whistle rising and falling on its own while you hold the key.

steps.title: Fade in and out
steps.why:
ENV 1, the loudness envelope, now fades the wind in and out, so it arrives and leaves like weather instead of switching on.
- ENV 1 attack 7 (610 ms): about half a second to reach full level.
- ENV 1 decay 7 (2.1 s, release 1.7 s): with full sustain this only acts after you let go. On the SEM, DECAY also sets the release, so the wind dies away over almost two seconds.
- ENV 1 sustain 10 (100 %): the wind holds at full for as long as the key is down.
- Listen for: tap a key and hear the gust swell and fade. Hold a key for a long, gusting wind.

sounds.name: Parallel Harmony Lead
sounds.ref: A patchbay lesson: one module playing the other’s notes
sounds.blurb: A lead that plays every note twice, a major third apart, on the two modules.
sounds.how: CV 1 carries the pitch XM1 is playing. Patched into XM2’s VCO 1 CV, it drives both of XM2’s oscillators, so XM2 follows XM1 whatever ASSIGN says. XM2’s VCOs are tuned a major third up, so every note comes out as a harmony. ASSIGN is at SPLIT with the riff below middle C, so XM2 gets no keys of its own; only its envelope needs a gate, which comes from GATE 1.

steps.title: XM1: a bright lead
steps.why:
XM1 becomes a bright lead, and the keyboard is split so only XM1 gets your notes. XM2 will follow it through cables in the next step.
- ASSIGN SPLIT: keys below middle C go to XM1, the rest to XM2. The riff sits below middle C, so XM2 gets no keys of its own.
- VCO 1 −4 (saw 80 %), VCO 2 −3 (saw 60 %): the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) go into the VCF (filter) as two saws.
- VCO 2 fine tune +0.5 (+10 cents): a slight detune, so the note beats and sounds wider.
- VCF frequency 6.5 (1.7 kHz): low-pass, fairly open, so the lead stays bright but not harsh.
- ENV 1 decay 4.5 (350 ms, release 270 ms): with full sustain, notes hold and then fade over about a quarter of a second after you let go.
- Listen for: a bright, slightly chorused lead. Only XM1 sounds.

steps.title: Send XM1’s pitch and gate to XM2
steps.why:
Two cables make XM2 follow XM1. CV means control voltage: a signal that sets pitch or opens envelopes.
- Cable XM1 CV 1 → XM2 VCO 1 CV: CV 1 carries the pitch XM1 is playing. Into XM2’s VCO 1 CV, it drives both of XM2’s oscillators (VCO 2 follows unless it has a cable of its own), whatever ASSIGN says.
- Cable XM1 GATE 1 → XM2 ENV GATE: GATE 1 is high while XM1 plays a note. It fires XM2’s envelopes, since XM2 gets no keys of its own.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. XM2’s LEVEL is still at 0, so it plays along silently until the next step brings it up.

steps.title: Tune XM2 a third up
steps.why:
XM2 is tuned a major third up and brought in, so every note XM1 plays comes out as a two-note harmony.
- XM2 VCO 1 and 2 FREQ 5.7 (+4 st): four semitones, a major third. The knob is continuous, so intervals are set by ear: 5.5 would be a minor third, 6.17 a fifth.
- XM2 VCO 2 fine −0.5 (−10 cents): a slight detune against VCO 1 for width.
- XM2 VCO 1 pulse 60 %, VCO 2 saw 60 %: a pulse and a saw, so the harmony has a different colour from XM1’s two saws.
- XM2 VCF 6 (1.2 kHz), ENV 1 decay 4.5: a little darker than XM1, with the same release, so it sits behind the lead.
- XM2 level 6, pan +2.5: 60 %, 50 % to the right.
- Listen for: play the riff and hear a third above every note, a little to the right. Set XM2’s frequencies to 6.17 for parallel fifths.

sounds.name: Thin Reed
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s synth woodwind
sounds.blurb: A thin, nasal reed with a gentle vibrato.
sounds.how: NOTCH turned most of the way to the right makes the filter mostly high-pass, which removes the body of the sound and leaves a thin, reedy edge. A narrow pulse and a slow attack make it breathe like a wind instrument.

steps.title: A narrow pulse
steps.why:
A reed sound starts from a narrow pulse wave, which has a thin, nasal colour even before any filtering.
- VCO 1 into VCF +4 (pulse 80 %): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Its knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre; right of centre sends the pulse wave.
- VCO 1 pulse width 25 %: at 50 % the pulse is a square, hollow like a clarinet. Narrower, it thins to a nasal, reedy tone like an oboe. Further towards 10 % it goes buzzy and weak.
- Listen for: a thin, nasal tone. Sweep PULSE WIDTH between 50 % and 25 % to hear it go from hollow to reedy.

steps.title: Mostly high-pass
steps.why:
The SEM’s NOTCH knob sweeps the filter from low-pass through notch to high-pass. Turned well to the right it mostly removes the lows, which takes the body out of the note and leaves a thin, reedy edge.
- VCF notch +3 (20 % LP, 80 % HP): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is now mostly high-pass. Turn it left and the sound gets fuller; fully right and it gets thinner still.
- VCF frequency 5.4 (788 Hz): where the cut sits. In high-pass, higher is thinner; around 800 Hz the low body is gone but the note still has pitch.
- VCF resonance 3 (30 %): a slight lift at the cutoff that adds a nasal honk.
- Listen for: the note losing its bottom and turning papery and nasal. Turn NOTCH back towards the left to hear the body return.

steps.title: Breathe in
steps.why:
ENV 1 shapes the loudness through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). A slower attack makes each note start the way a breath does, instead of clicking on.
- ENV 1 attack 5.5 (200 ms): a fifth of a second to reach full level. Shorter sounds tongued and hard; longer, too slow for a melody.
- ENV 1 decay 5 (500 ms, release 390 ms): with full sustain it only acts after you let go. On the SEM, DECAY also sets the release, so notes tail off smoothly.
- ENV 1 sustain 10 (100 %): the note holds at full while the key is down, like a held breath.
- Listen for: notes that swell in and trail off rather than switch on and off. Play legato to hear them join.

steps.title: Vibrato
steps.why:
XM1’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator, a slow wave that moves a setting) adds a gentle vibrato, the waver a wind player puts on a long note.
- VCO 1 modulation −0.8 (FM +0.6 st): left of centre moves pitch (FREQ; FM means frequency modulation). A touch left is a subtle vibrato; further left gets wobbly. Right of centre would move pulse width instead.
- VCO 1 modulation source LFO: the switch starts at ENV 1.
- XM1 LFO rate 6.1 (4.69 Hz): just under five wobbles a second, a natural woodwind speed.
- Listen for: long notes wavering slightly in pitch. Set MODULATION to the centre and the reed goes flat and electronic.

sounds.name: Gated Pulse
sounds.ref: A patchbay lesson: an LFO firing the envelopes
sounds.blurb: Held notes chopped into a steady stream of plucks by the other module’s LFO.
sounds.how: XM2’s LFO is patched into XM1’s ENV GATE, so XM1’s envelopes fire every time the LFO rises, not when a key goes down. Hold a key and it becomes a pulsing rhythm; XM2’s LFO knob sets the tempo. XM2 itself stays silent.

steps.title: A plucky XM1
steps.why:
XM1 is set up as a short, resonant pluck. The envelopes will be fired by a cable later instead of by the keys, so the sound itself needs to be short and clear.
- VCO 1 saw 80 %, VCO 2 pulse 60 %: the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) mixed by their knobs in the VCF section, saw to the left, pulse to the right.
- VCO 2 frequency 7 (+12 st): the pulse an octave up, for a bright top.
- FREQ 3.5 (216 Hz), RES 5: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in low-pass, dark with a clear ring.
- VCF MOD +3.3 oct, ENV 2 D 210 ms, S 0: ENV 2 flicks the filter open on each note and shuts it.
- ENV 1 decay 4 (250 ms), sustain 0: ENV 1, the loudness envelope, lets each note die away by itself.
- Listen for: a short, bright pluck on each key. Held keys do not keep sounding.

steps.title: Fire the envelopes from XM2’s LFO
steps.why:
XM2’s LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow triangle wave, is patched into XM1’s ENV GATE, the input that fires XM1’s envelopes from outside. XM2 itself stays silent; only its LFO is used.
- Cable XM2 LFO → XM1 ENV GATE: XM1’s envelopes now fire each time the LFO rises, in place of the key. The keys still set the pitch.
- XM2 LFO rate: still at its starting 2.35 Hz, a little over two plucks a second.
- Listen for: hold a key and it turns into a steady stream of plucks. Change the note and the stream carries on at the new pitch.

steps.title: Set the tempo
steps.why:
XM2’s LFO knob is now the tempo control for XM1’s plucks.
- XM2 LFO rate 5.4 (3.02 Hz): about three plucks a second. Faster packs them closer; slower spaces them out. Each pluck needs to be shorter than the gap between them, which at this speed is about 330 ms, so the 210 ms filter and 250 ms loudness envelopes fit.
- Listen for: hold a key and turn XM2’s LFO rate up. When the plucks come faster than ENV 1 can die away, they start to run into each other. Lengthen XM1’s ENV 2 decay to hear the same smearing.

sounds.name: Open Fifths Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Vangelis-era analogue pads
sounds.blurb: A broad, warm pad in open fifths that swells in slowly.
sounds.how: Each module has VCO 2 tuned a fifth above VCO 1, so a single key already sounds like an open chord, and UNI plays it on both modules at once. XM2 is detuned slightly against XM1 and panned the other way, which spreads the pad across the stereo.

steps.title: Fifths in each module
steps.why:
Each module gets VCO 2 tuned a fifth above VCO 1, so a single key sounds like an open chord. Only XM1 is heard for now; XM2 is set up the same, ready for the next step.
- VCO 1 saw 70 %, VCO 2 saw 60 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The knobs in the VCF (filter) section are silent at the centre and send the sawtooth to the left.
- VCO 2 frequency 6.2 (+7 st): seven semitones, a perfect fifth. The knob is continuous, so the fifth sits at about 6.17; set it by ear until the beating stops.
- Listen for: each key playing a root and fifth together, a hollow, open sound with no major or minor colour.

steps.title: Both modules on every note
steps.why:
UNI plays each note on both modules. XM2 is tuned a little flat of XM1 and the two are panned wide, so the pad spreads across the stereo and moves.
- ASSIGN UNI: both modules on every note, where the switch starts.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): up from 0, so XM2 now sounds with XM1.
- XM1 pan −3.5, XM2 pan +3.5: 70 % to opposite sides, for a wide pad.
- XM2 fine −10 and −8 cents: XM2 slightly flat, so it beats slowly against XM1 and the pad swirls between the speakers.
- Listen for: a wide, gently moving chord. Set XM2’s fine tunes to 0 and the movement stops.

steps.title: Warm filters
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is brought down for warmth, and ENV 2, the filter envelope, opens it slowly over each note, so the pad gets brighter as you hold it.
- FREQ 4.5 (427 Hz), RES 2: low-pass part way down, round and warm, with a slight lift at the cutoff.
- VCF modulation +2 (+1.8 oct): how far ENV 2 opens the filter at its peak.
- ENV 2 A 900 ms, D 2.1 s, S 60 %: nearly a second to open, then over two seconds to settle to 60 %, so the brightness blooms and eases back.
- Listen for: hold a chord and hear it brighten slowly after the note starts. Set ENV 2 attack to 0 on both and the opening becomes a quick flash.

steps.title: Slow swell
steps.why:
ENV 1, the loudness envelope, makes each note swell in and fade out slowly: the classic pad shape.
- ENV 1 attack 7.3 (770 ms): about three quarters of a second to reach full level. It arrives just before the filter’s 900 ms peak, so the tone brightens as it swells.
- ENV 1 decay 7 (2.1 s, release 1.7 s): with full sustain it only acts after you let go. On the SEM, DECAY also sets the release, so chords fade over nearly two seconds.
- ENV 1 sustain 10 (100 %): full level while held, on both modules.
- Listen for: chords rising gently out of silence and hanging after you let go. Change chords before the tail ends and they overlap.

context.xm2_vco1.fine: In this sound: the slight detune against XM1 that makes the pad move.

sounds.name: Band-Pass Clav
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s funk clavinet parts
sounds.blurb: A short, nasal, plucked keyboard sound for funky two-note stabs.
sounds.how: The band-pass filter keeps only the middle of a narrow pulse wave, which gives the nasal, clavinet-like tone. Short envelopes with no sustain make every note a pluck. DUO lets two notes sound at once, one on each module.

steps.title: A narrow pulse, band-pass
steps.why:
The clavinet tone comes from a narrow pulse through the band-pass filter, which keeps only the middle of the sound. Both modules get the same settings; only XM1 is heard until step 3.
- VCO 1 into VCF +4 (pulse 80 %): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Its knob in the VCF section is silent at the centre and sends the pulse to the right.
- VCO 1 pulse width 20 %: very narrow, so the tone is thin and nasal, the clavinet edge.
- VCF response BP: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) switches to BP, band-pass: only a band around the cutoff gets through.
- FREQ 6.3 (1.5 kHz), RES 3: where the nasal band sits, slightly emphasised. Higher is thinner and sharper.
- Listen for: a thin, honky, nasal note with no low end. Sweep FREQUENCY to hear it change vowel.

steps.title: Pluck it
steps.why:
Short envelopes with no sustain make every note a pluck, the way a clavinet string is struck and damped.
- VCF modulation +2 (+1.8 oct): how far ENV 2, the filter envelope, lifts the band at the start of each note.
- ENV 2 decay 4 (250 ms), sustain 0: the band opens at once and falls back in a quarter of a second. Shorter is a clickier “tik”.
- ENV 1 D 330 ms, S 0: ENV 1, the loudness envelope, lets each note die away by itself in about a third of a second.
- Listen for: a percussive “plink” that dies quickly. Play a choppy sixteenth-note riff and it stays tight.

steps.title: Two notes at once
steps.why:
DUO shares notes between the two modules, so two-note funk stabs play one note on each.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free. Hold two keys and XM1 and XM2 take one each. UNI would stack both modules on every note.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): up from 0, so XM2’s matching clav is heard.
- Listen for: two-note stabs sounding as a pair. Both modules sit in the centre, so the pair sounds like one instrument.

context.xm1_vco1.pulse_width: In this sound: the narrow pulse that gives the clavinet edge.

tweaks.hear: From a dry click to a ringing pluck.

sounds.name: The Tuning Tone
sounds.ref: Getting to know the 2-XM’s built-in A440
sounds.blurb: A melody played over a steady A, using the tuning tone that the EXT input carries when nothing is plugged in.
sounds.how: With no cable in XM1’s EXT jack, turning the EXT knob towards IN brings in a steady 440 Hz tone, meant for tuning. It goes through the filter and the envelopes like the oscillators, so it only sounds while a note is held, but it never changes pitch. Here it becomes a drone under the melody.

steps.title: Bring in the tuning tone
steps.why:
With nothing plugged into XM1’s EXT jack, the EXT input carries a steady 440 Hz tuning tone, an A. Bringing it into the filter puts that A under every note.
- EXT/noise knob −3 (in 60 %): the third knob in the VCF (filter) section is silent at the centre, brings in the external input to the left and white noise to the right. Left, with no cable, gives the tuning tone. At the centre the drone disappears.
- XM1 EXT level 7 (70 %): how loud the tone is. It is only heard with the EXT knob turned towards IN.
- Listen for: a steady A under every note, whatever key you press. It passes through the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) like the oscillators, so it only sounds while a key is held.

steps.title: A soft melody on top
steps.why:
The melody on top is softened so the tuning tone and the tune sit together.
- VCO 1 into VCF +3 (pulse 60 %): VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Right of centre sends the pulse, still at 50 % width, which makes a square: hollow and gentle.
- VCF frequency 6.2 (1.4 kHz): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in low-pass comes down from 4.6 kHz and rounds off both the square and the A.
- ENV 1 attack 3 (29 ms): a soft start with no click.
- ENV 1 D 720 ms, S 100 %: notes hold, then fade over about half a second after you let go.
- Listen for: melodies over the A, clashing on some notes and settling on others. Play in A minor or A major for the drone to sit well.

sounds.name: Drone and Melody
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s electronic soundtrack cues
sounds.blurb: A low, humming drone under a vocal-sounding melody, one on each module.
sounds.how: SPLIT gives the low key to XM1 and the melody to XM2. XM1 has a slow LFO moving its notch filter, for a slowly changing drone. XM2 uses the band-pass filter with resonance, which gives the melody a vowel-like quality.

steps.title: Split, both modules
steps.why:
SPLIT turns the two modules into two instruments: XM1 plays the low drone key, XM2 the melody above it.
- ASSIGN SPLIT: keys below middle C play XM1, the rest play XM2. UNI would put both on every note; DUO would share them out as you play.
- XM2 level 6.5 (65 %): XM2 starts at 0; at 6.5 it sits just under XM1.
- Listen for: low and high keys sounding the same for now, the plain starting sawtooth, until each module gets its own sound.

steps.title: XM1: a slowly moving drone
steps.why:
XM1 becomes a low, humming drone whose tone keeps changing on its own, because its LFO slowly moves a notch-like filter.
- Saws 80 % and 60 %, VCO 2 −12 st: the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) as two saws, the second an octave down for weight.
- VCF notch −1 (60 % LP, 40 % HP): the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) NOTCH knob just left of centre, between low-pass and notch, so it scoops the sound while keeping some low end.
- FREQ 4.5 (427 Hz), RES 4: where the scoop sits, with enough emphasis to hear it.
- VCF MOD LFO, +2.5 oct at 0.35 Hz: the LFO (low-frequency oscillator) sweeps the cutoff about every three seconds.
- ENV 1 A 130 ms, D 2.1 s, S 100 %: a soft start, full hold, a long fade.
- Listen for: a low note whose tone slowly shifts from hollow to full.

steps.title: XM2: a vocal melody
steps.why:
XM2 plays the melody through the band-pass filter with resonance, which picks out one area of the sound and gives it a vowel-like colour.
- XM2 VCO 1 +3.5 (pulse 70 %): a square at 50 % width, hollow and simple, so the filter does the talking.
- XM2 VCF response BP, FREQ 6.2 (1.4 kHz): band-pass lets only a band around the cutoff through. The cutoff sets the vowel: lower is “oo”, higher towards “ee”.
- XM2 VCF resonance 6 (60 %): strong emphasis, which makes the vowel stand out.
- XM2 ENV 1 A 63 ms, D 720 ms, S 100 %: a soft, sung start and a half-second tail.
- XM2 VCO 1 FM +0.6 st, LFO 3.89 Hz: left of centre is pitch (FM means frequency modulation), a gentle vibrato from XM2’s own LFO.
- Listen for: a singing line over the drone. Sweep XM2’s FREQUENCY to change the vowel.

sounds.name: Velvet Electric Piano
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s soft-rock electric piano
sounds.blurb: A warm, rounded electric piano that plays two-note chords, one note on each module, and gets brighter the harder you play.
sounds.how: Each module plays one note of a two-note chord (DUO). A square wave through a low 12 dB filter is soft and round, and a quiet sawtooth two octaves up gives the piano its metallic edge. The filter modulation switch at EXT, with nothing in the VCF CV jack, uses ENV 2 scaled by velocity, and the VCA at E+V does the same for loudness: harder notes are brighter and louder, as on a real electric piano.

steps.title: One note per module
steps.why:
The 2-XM is two separate synths, XM1 and XM2. DUO gives each note of a two-note chord its own module, which is how this electric piano plays intervals rather than single notes.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free. Hold two keys and XM1 takes one, XM2 the other.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0, silent whatever its panel does. At 7 it matches XM1.
- XM1 pan −2, XM2 pan +2: 40 % to each side, so the two notes of a chord sit slightly apart, like the spread of a real instrument.
- Listen for: hold two keys and hear both, one a little left and one a little right, still on the modules’ plain starting sawtooth.

steps.title: A square and a quiet high sawtooth
steps.why:
The piano tone starts from a soft square with a faint sawtooth two octaves above it. The square is the round body; the high saw is the metallic edge of an electric piano’s tine.
- VCO 1 +3 (pulse 60 %), PW 50 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Right of centre on its knob in the VCF (filter) section sends the pulse, and at 50 % that is a square: hollow and round.
- VCO 2 into VCF −1.5 (saw 30 %): only a little towards SAW, so it colours rather than dominates. At the centre the piano is plainer and softer.
- VCO 2 frequency 9 (+24 st): two octaves up. On FREQUENCY two numbers is an octave, so 9 is four above the starting 5.
- Listen for: a hollow tone with a thin, glassy shimmer on top. Turn VCO 2’s knob to the centre on one module to hear the edge disappear.

steps.title: A velocity-scaled filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) sets the brightness, and here it follows how hard you play. The EXT position of its modulation switch, with no cable in VCF CV, gives ENV 2 scaled by velocity.
- FREQ 4.4 (399 Hz), RES 1: low-pass at about 400 Hz, dark and warm at rest, with barely any emphasis.
- VCF modulation source EXT: ENV 2 (the filter envelope) times velocity. Soft notes barely open the filter; hard ones open it fully.
- VCF modulation +2.6 (+2.6 oct): how much brighter a hard note is than a soft one.
- ENV 2 A 0, D 580 ms, S 10 %: the brightness arrives at once and fades over about half a second, as a struck tine does.
- Listen for: play softly, then hard. Soft notes are mellow and round; hard ones bark with a bright edge that dies back.

steps.title: A piano’s fade
steps.why:
The VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) sets loudness. At E+V it also follows how hard you play, and ENV 1 is turned into a slow fade with no hold, so every note dies away by itself like a struck key.
- VCA mode E+V: ENV 1 scaled by velocity, so soft notes are quieter, like a real key.
- ENV 1 attack 0 (3 ms): the note starts at once, with a clear strike.
- ENV 1 decay 7 (2.1 s, release 1.7 s): how long each note rings. On the SEM DECAY is the release too, so notes ring on after you let go.
- ENV 1 sustain 0: nothing is held, so long notes fade out over two seconds even with the key down.
- Listen for: chords that ring and fade away evenly. Play a soft note after a hard one and hear it both quieter and darker.

sounds.name: Layered Tine Piano
sounds.ref: Two different voices on every note
sounds.blurb: A soft piano body from one module and a glassy, ringing tine from the other, played together on every key.
sounds.how: UNI plays each key on both modules, and the two modules are set up as two different instruments. XM1 is the body: a square through a low-pass filter with a long fade. XM2 is only the tine: a sawtooth two octaves up through the band-pass filter, with a short, bright decay. Layered, they sound like one struck note with a bell in it. A single synth with one filter could not give the two parts different filters and different envelopes.

steps.title: Both modules on every key
steps.why:
UNI plays each key on both modules at once, and in this sound the two modules become two different instruments stacked on one note.
- ASSIGN UNI: every key goes to both XM1 and XM2. It is where the switch starts.
- XM2 level 5.5 (55 %): up from 0, a little below XM1’s 7, because XM2 will only be the tine on top.
- XM1 pan −1.5, XM2 pan +1.5: 30 % to each side, a slight spread between body and tine.
- Listen for: the note a little louder and wider. Both modules are still on their starting sawtooth.

steps.title: XM1: the body
steps.why:
XM1 becomes the piano body: a square through a low filter, a small bump of brightness at the strike, and a two-second fade.
- VCO 1 +3.5 (pulse 70 %), PW 50 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Right of centre sends the pulse; at 50 % it is a square, round and hollow.
- VCF frequency 4.6 (457 Hz), resonance 0: the VCF (voltage-controlled filter) in low-pass, warm and plain.
- VCF MOD +1.5 oct, ENV 2 D 720 ms, S 10 %: ENV 2, the filter envelope, opens the filter at the strike and lets it close.
- ENV 1 A 0, D 2.1 s, S 0: ENV 1, the loudness envelope, fades each note over two seconds, even held.
- Listen for: a soft, round piano note that dies away. XM2’s plain saw is still on top, which the next step turns into the tine.

steps.title: XM2: the tine
steps.why:
XM2 becomes only the tine: a sawtooth two octaves up, through the band-pass filter, so just a narrow, glassy band is left.
- XM2 VCO 1 into VCF −4 (saw 80 %): the saw carries every harmonic, so the band-pass has plenty to pick from.
- XM2 VCO 1 frequency 9 (+24 st): two octaves above the body. 8.17 would put it an octave and a fifth up, for more of a bell.
- XM2 VCF response BP: band-pass lets through only a band around the cutoff.
- XM2 FREQ 7 (2.3 kHz), RES 5: where the glassy band sits, with enough resonance to make it ring.
- Listen for: a thin, whistling tone above the piano that still holds on while you keep the key down. The next step makes it short.

steps.title: A short ring for the tine
steps.why:
XM2’s ENV 1 is shortened so the tine rings only at the start of each note and leaves the body to fade on its own. Two filters and two envelopes on one note is something a single-filter synth cannot do.
- XM2 ENV 1 attack 0 (3 ms): the tine arrives with the strike.
- XM2 ENV 1 D 380 ms: about a third of a second of ring. Longer turns the piano into a celesta.
- XM2 ENV 1 sustain 0: the tine always dies away by itself.
- Listen for: a bright “ting” on each note that fades well before the body. Turn XM2 level up and down to change how much tine is layered in.

sounds.name: Soft Mallets
sounds.ref: In the style of a marimba played in thirds
sounds.blurb: Round, woody mallet notes, two at a time, one on each side.
sounds.how: A square wave through a low, slightly resonant filter that ENV 2 flicks open gives a soft knock with a clear pitch. A faint sawtooth two octaves up adds the ring a tuned bar has. DUO plays two-note intervals on the two modules, panned apart, like a player with a mallet in each hand.

steps.title: Two mallets
steps.why:
Two mallets need two voices. DUO plays each note of an interval on its own module, and panning puts one mallet on each side.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free, so two notes of a third sound together, one per module.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0; at 7 it matches XM1.
- XM1 pan −2.5, XM2 pan +2.5: 50 % to each side, like a player with a mallet in each hand.
- Listen for: hold two keys and hear one on each side, still on the plain starting sawtooth.

steps.title: A square and a faint ring
steps.why:
The bar’s tone starts from a square with a faint sawtooth two octaves above it. The square gives a clear, woody pitch; the high saw adds the ring a tuned bar has.
- VCO 1 +4 (pulse 80 %), PW 50 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Right of centre on its knob in the VCF (filter) section sends the pulse; at 50 % it is a square.
- VCO 2 into VCF −1 (saw 20 %): only a little towards SAW, a faint upper ring.
- VCO 2 frequency 9 (+24 st): two octaves up.
- Listen for: a hollow note with a faint whistle above it. Turn VCO 2’s knob to the centre and the ring goes.

steps.title: A soft knock
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set low and ENV 2, the filter envelope, flicks it open on each note: a soft knock with a clear pitch.
- FREQ 4.2 (348 Hz), RES 2.5: low-pass, dark at rest, with a slight lift at the cutoff for a woody tone.
- VCF modulation +2.2 (+2.0 oct): how far ENV 2 opens the filter at the strike.
- ENV 2 A 0, D 380 ms, S 0: an instant knock that closes in about a third of a second. Shorter is a softer, woodier mallet; longer sounds harder.
- Listen for: a “tok” at the start of each note, then a round, dark tone. Sweep ENV 2 decay to change the mallet from felt to rubber.

steps.title: A short decay
steps.why:
ENV 1, the loudness envelope, now lets each note ring and die away by itself, as a struck bar does.
- ENV 1 attack 0 (3 ms): the note starts with the strike.
- ENV 1 decay 5.8 (890 ms, release 700 ms): just under a second of ring. Longer turns wood into metal, closer to a vibraphone.
- ENV 1 sustain 0: nothing is held, so holding the key does not make the note last longer.
- Listen for: short, woody notes that fade within a second. Play a quick run of thirds and hear them bounce from side to side.

sounds.name: Harmonium
sounds.ref: In the style of a pump organ
sounds.blurb: A soft, reedy organ that breathes into each note and plays two-note harmonies.
sounds.how: A narrow pulse sounds like a free reed, and a sawtooth an octave below adds the low stop. The attack is slow enough to sound pumped rather than switched. DUO gives each note of a harmony its own module, and the two are detuned very slightly, like real reeds.

steps.title: Two reeds
steps.why:
DUO gives each note of a harmony its own module, and XM2 is tuned a few cents flat so the two reeds beat gently, like real reeds.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to whichever module is free; hold two keys and XM1 and XM2 take one each.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0; at 7 it matches XM1.
- XM1 pan −1.5, XM2 pan +1.5: 30 % to each side, close together like one instrument.
- XM2 VCO 1 fine tune −0.3 (−6 cents): a tiny bit flat, too little to sound out of tune.
- Listen for: two notes at once, with a very slow waver between them.

steps.title: A narrow pulse and a low stop
steps.why:
A narrow pulse sounds like a free reed, and a sawtooth an octave below adds the low stop, as pulling a stop on a harmonium does.
- VCO 1 +3.5 (pulse 70 %), PW 30 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Right of centre in the VCF (filter) section sends the pulse. At 30 % it is narrower than a square, more nasal; 50 % would be a hollow clarinet.
- VCO 2 −2.5 (saw 50 %), FREQ 3 (−12 st): the low stop, an octave down.
- VCO 2 fine tune +0.3 (+6 cents): a slight detune on each module, so the octave beats slowly.
- Listen for: a reedy, buzzing note with body underneath. Turn VCO 2’s knob to the centre to hear the stop drop out.

steps.title: A soft filter
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) softens the reeds, and ENV 2 opens it slightly as each note fills with air.
- FREQ 5.3 (736 Hz), RES 1.5: low-pass in the middle, so the buzz is tamed but the reed colour stays.
- VCF modulation +0.8 (+0.4 oct): only a small lift from ENV 2, the filter envelope.
- ENV 2 A 92 ms, D 1.0 s, S 60 %: the filter opens over about a tenth of a second and settles slowly, a slight brightening as the bellows push.
- Listen for: each note getting slightly brighter just after it starts. It is subtle; set VCF modulation to 0 to compare.

steps.title: Pumped in
steps.why:
ENV 1, the loudness envelope, is slowed at the start so notes sound pumped in by a bellows rather than switched on.
- ENV 1 attack 4.2 (73 ms): the breath at the start of each note. Longer gives a lazier pump; 0 sounds like an electronic organ.
- ENV 1 decay 5 (500 ms, release 390 ms): with full sustain it only acts after you let go. On the SEM DECAY also sets the release, so notes tail off rather than stop.
- ENV 1 sustain 10 (100 %): full level while the key is down.
- Listen for: hymn-like two-note harmonies that breathe in and die away smoothly.

sounds.name: Ping-Pong Arpeggio
sounds.ref: DUO and PAN: an arpeggio that bounces across the stereo
sounds.blurb: A soft plucked arpeggio whose notes land left, right, left, right, each ringing on under the next.
sounds.how: In DUO each new key goes to the module that has been free longest, so the notes of an arpeggio alternate between XM1 and XM2. Pan the two modules hard apart and the arpeggio bounces from side to side. Each note has a long fade, so it is still ringing on one side when the next note starts on the other. No effects are involved: the stereo comes from the two voices.

steps.title: DUO, panned hard apart
steps.why:
DUO hands each new note to the other module, and the two modules are panned hard apart, so an arpeggio bounces from side to side. No effects are involved: the stereo comes from the two voices.
- ASSIGN DUO: each new key goes to the module that has been free longest, so the notes of an arpeggio alternate XM1, XM2.
- XM2 level 7 (70 %): XM2 starts at 0; at 7 it matches XM1.
- XM1 pan −4.5, XM2 pan +4.5: 90 % to each side, nearly hard left and right. Bring both towards the centre for a narrower bounce.
- Listen for: play an arpeggio and hear notes land left, right, left, right.

steps.title: A soft pulse with an octave
steps.why:
Each module gets a soft pulse with a quieter sawtooth an octave up, for a gentle but clear pluck.
- VCO 1 +3.5 (pulse 70 %), PW 40 %: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Right of centre in the VCF (filter) section sends the pulse. At 40 % it is a little narrower than a square, slightly more nasal.
- VCO 2 −2 (saw 40 %), FREQ 7 (+12 st): a saw an octave up, a little towards SAW, for sparkle.
- Listen for: a hollow note with a brighter octave on top. Turn VCO 2’s knob to the centre and it loses its shine.

steps.title: A rounded pluck
steps.why:
The VCF (voltage-controlled filter) is set low, and ENV 2, the filter envelope, opens it at the start of each note and closes it in half a second: a rounded pluck.
- FREQ 4.2 (348 Hz), RES 3: low-pass, dark at rest, with some emphasis for a slight rubbery edge.
- VCF modulation +2.4 (+2.3 oct): the brightness of each pluck.
- ENV 2 A 0, D 500 ms, S 0: opens at once, closes in half a second, holds nothing.
- Listen for: each note starting bright and mellowing. Sweep VCF modulation to make the plucks harder or softer.

steps.title: Long tails
steps.why:
ENV 1, the loudness envelope, is given a long tail with no hold, so each note is still ringing on its side when the next one starts on the other.
- ENV 1 attack 0 (3 ms): each note lands on time.
- ENV 1 decay 6.8 (1.8 s, release 1.4 s): nearly two seconds of ring, and on the SEM DECAY is also the release, so notes ring on after you let go. Shorter makes the bounce drier.
- ENV 1 sustain 0: every note fades by itself.
- Listen for: an arpeggio that fills both speakers, the notes overlapping across the stereo. Shorten DECAY to hear it turn into separate blips.
